title: A 'Second Moon' Briefly Lingers by Earth: 2-Meter Asteroid to Depart in January 2027

content:
A roughly 2-meter-diameter asteroid, 2026 QQ8, has been captured by Earth's gravity since April and is orbiting the planet, and is expected to escape Earth's gravitational sphere in January 2027 and return to a solar orbit. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center gave the object its official designation in late October. Early on, it was difficult to distinguish from satellite debris, but follow-up observations confirmed it is a natural object. Its closest approach to Earth is estimated at about 570,000 km, so there is no collision risk, and even if it entered the atmosphere, most of it would burn up. On average, roughly one minimoon is estimated to exist around Earth at any given time.

A "second moon" orbiting Earth has been confirmed. An asteroid just over 2 meters in diameter has been captured by Earth's gravity and has been circling the planet for seven months, and is expected to escape Earth's gravitational sphere in January 2027.

The International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center (MPC) gave the object the official designation "2026 QQ8" in late October. Krisztián Sárneczky, a research coordinator at Hungary's Konkoly Observatory, first discovered it in August, when it carried the provisional designation "Sar2901." Immediately after discovery, it appeared no different from previously observed near-Earth asteroids, but precise orbital calculations revealed that it had been captured by Earth's gravity. Earth is believed to have captured the object in April.

2026 QQ8 belongs to the category of near-Earth objects (NEOs) known as "minimoons"—natural objects temporarily captured by Earth. Minimoon is not a formally recognized academic term, but it is an expression astronomers have conventionally used to describe objects that spend a short time in Earth's orbit. Past examples include 2006 RH120, which circled Earth for about a year, and 2020 CD3, which orbited Earth for about three years.

Only six minimoons, including 2026 QQ8, have been confirmed as natural objects to date.

Confirming the identity of this object took considerable time. Because it is so small and faint, it was difficult to distinguish from defunct satellites or their debris using visual and optical observations alone. Astronomers only leaned toward a natural origin after tracking for several weeks how solar radiation affected the object's motion, and follow-up observations using the Lowell Discovery Telescope in Arizona and the 2.2-meter telescope at Mauna Kea Observatory in Hawaii ultimately confirmed that it is a natural object, not artificial.

Immediately after discovery, some even speculated that it was a component related to the Apollo 13 mission in April 1970. Back-calculating its orbit indicated that the object passed near Earth between April 10 and 20, 1970. However, the MPC said in an asteroid electronic circular (MPEC 2026-U95) on October 29 that "no association with any known artificial object has been confirmed." Still, this is not an active proof that it is not artificial, but a passive determination that no evidence of it being artificial was found. The MPC strongly recommended further observations and dynamical studies.

2026 QQ8 is not expected to collide with Earth. While captured by Earth, its closest approach to the planet is estimated at about 570,000 km, farther than the average Earth-Moon distance of about 380,000 km. Even if it entered Earth's atmosphere, its small size means most of it would burn up and break apart without causing significant damage. Matthew Payne, director of the MPC, said it would amount to "at most a bright meteor appearing in the sky and a small booming sound."

Minimoons are by no means a rare phenomenon. Payne said, "On average, roughly one minimoon is estimated to exist around Earth at any given time," explaining that "sometimes they stay for weeks to months, sometimes there are none at all, and sometimes two or so exist at the same time." The reason records are sparse is that most are extremely small and are either far from Earth or moving at high speed, making them very difficult to detect with current observation systems.

For an object to be captured by Earth, two conditions must be met simultaneously. First, it must leave the region dominated by the Sun's gravity and enter the "Hill sphere," where Earth's gravity prevails. Earth's Hill sphere has a radius of about 1.5 million km, four times the Moon's orbit (about 380,000 km on average). Second, its speed must be sufficiently slow. Objects in orbits similar to Earth's have a low relative velocity with respect to Earth and are therefore easier to capture. A 2012 supercomputer simulation found that 18,000 of 10 million hypothetical near-Earth asteroids were temporarily captured. Capture and release occur mainly near the Lagrange points L1 and L2 of the Sun-Earth system.

Research is ongoing into the exact origin of 2026 QQ8. Most near-Earth objects are believed to originate in the asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. This region contains millions of rocky bodies of various sizes orbiting the Sun, and over millions of years of gravitational interactions, some migrate inward into the solar system. Payne explained that when a near-Earth object approaches at a speed not too fast to pass by, it can be influenced by the gravity of Earth and the Moon, gradually deviate from its original orbit, and enter an orbit around Earth.

Not all minimoons come from the asteroid belt, however. A study published in January 2025 suggested that 2024 PT5, which was a minimoon for just over two months starting in September 2024, may be debris ejected from the lunar surface by an impact. Spectroscopic observations of 2022 NX1 matched a K-type asteroid—neither lunar debris nor artificial.

The object is expected to approach Earth roughly every 10 years going forward. It also passed near Earth in 1965 but did not come close enough to be captured, and it will approach again in 2058 but is not expected to be captured as it was this time.

Astronomers have identified about 40,000 near-Earth objects to date, while about 1.5 million objects have been cataloged across the entire solar system. That number is expected to grow substantially as observational capacity expands. At Chile's Vera C. Rubin Observatory, a 10-year "Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST)" project is underway using a telescope equipped with the world's largest digital camera. Payne predicted that once the project is fully operational, the number of detectable objects will expand from the current 1.5 million to around 5 million.

This case is significant in that it has once again confirmed the existence of small objects moving in and out of Earth's gravitational sphere. As observation technology advances, the frequency of minimoon detections is expected to rise further, and this is expected to serve as basic data for understanding the orbits and origins of near-Earth objects.
